For example: @CaptainZoro walking through a futuristic city.'

findings.claim: F17: Flow's help pages contradict each other on whether a paid plan is required. Everyone gets 50 credits a day, plans add monthly credits, and image credit costs are not published in the help center.
findings.detail: Get-started page: 'Currently, to use Google Flow, you must meet all of these requirements: ... 18 years of age or older... supported regions... Be subscribed to Google AI Plus, Google AI Pro, or Google AI Ultra.' Credits page: 'With or without a subscription, you receive 50 Google Flow credits per day.' Plus gets an extra 200 credits a month, Pro 1,000, Ultra $100 10,000 and Ultra $200 25,000. Non-subscribers may be blocked from video at peak hours but 'can still generate images'. On costs: 'You can find the latest costs in the product when you select a model'. Rate limits apply 'particularly for zero-credit models'. Vietnam is a supported country and Vietnamese a supported language.

findings.claim: F18: Whisk was discontinued on 30 April 2026 and its features moved into Flow. ImageFX also moved into Flow, and third-party reports say it shut down the same day.
findings.detail: Workspace Updates (2026-03-12): 'the best capabilities from Whisk are moving directly into Flow'. Whisk was discontinued on April 30, 2026, and media left in a Whisk library 'will be permanently deleted'. The Flow update post (2026-02-25) says Nano Banana is built into Flow, that 'you can generate images for free in Flow' (this free claim may be outdated, see F15/F17), and that Whisk and ImageFX users could migrate. The ImageFX shutdown date comes from third-party reports only.

findings.claim: F19: Google's official best practices: be hyper-specific, state context and intent, iterate in small steps, give step-by-step instructions for complex scenes, write 'semantic negative prompts' (describe what you want instead of 'no X'), and direct the camera.
findings.detail: API doc quotes: 'Be hyper-specific: The more detail you provide, the more control you have.' 'Provide context and intent: Explain the purpose of the image.' 'Iterate and refine... "Keep everything the same, but change the character's expression to be more serious."' 'Use step-by-step instructions: For complex scenes with many elements, break your prompt into steps. "First, create a background... Then... Finally..."' 'Use "semantic negative prompts": Instead of saying "no cars," describe the intended scene positively: "an empty, deserted street with no signs of traffic."' 'Control the camera: Use photographic and cinematic language'. The Cloud guide says the same: 'Describe what you want, not what you don't want'.

findings.claim: F20: Official prompt formulas: Subject + Action + Location/context + Composition + Style, with a separate template for illustrations. For history, Google suggests stating the accuracy requirement explicitly and checking the result.
findings.detail: Cloud guide (2026-03-06): 'Formula: [Subject] + [Action] + [Location/context] + [Composition] + [Style]'. API illustration template: 'A [style] of a [subject, with details about accessories or actions] doing [activity]. The design features [visual qualities, e.g., bold outlines, cel-shading, etc.] and [color/background preference].' with the note 'Be specific about the visual detail (bold lines, colors, etc.) for consistent results.' Consumer FAQ: 'Try <Create/generate an image of> <subject> <action> <scene>'. Nano Banana Pro tips: 'Factual constraints (for diagrams): Specify the need for accuracy... (e.g., ... "Ensure historical accuracy for the Victorian era.")' and 'Always verify the factual accuracy of data-driven visuals like diagrams and infographics.'

findings.claim: F21: Official editing templates: change only a named element and keep everything else, combine elements from specific numbered images, and describe critical features in detail so they survive the edit.
findings.detail: Inpainting: 'Using the provided image, change only the [specific element] to [new element/description]. Keep everything else in the image exactly the same, preserving the original style, lighting, and composition.' Composition: 'Take the [element from image 1] and place it with/on the [element from image 2].' High-fidelity preservation: 'To ensure critical details (like a face or logo) are preserved during an edit, describe them in great detail along with your edit request.' The Nano Banana Pro tips post says: 'For modifying an existing image, be direct and specific.'

findings.claim: F22: Google has no official 'character sheet' template. The closest guidance is the 360-view method (build angles one at a time, feeding earlier outputs back in), comic panels, and multi-character examples that state identity must stay fixed.
findings.detail: API, 'Character consistency: 360 view': 'generate 360-degree views of a character by iteratively prompting for different angles. For best results, include previously generated images in subsequent prompts to maintain consistency. For complex poses, include a reference image of the selected pose.' Template: 'A studio portrait of [person] against [background], [looking forward/in profile looking right/etc.]'. Sequential art: 'Make a 3 panel comic in a [style]...', which works 'best with Gemini 3 Pro and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image'. Nano Banana 2 post examples: 'Keep the attire and identity consistent of all 3 characters, but their expressions and angles should vary throughout all 6 images. Make sure to only have one of each character in each image. Generate 6 images one at a time. Each image should be a separate output in 16:9 format.' and 'It is strictly important to keep identity consistent of all the 14 characters and items.' I found no official multi-pose model-sheet guidance.

findings.claim: F23: Text inside images: put the exact words in quotes and describe the font. Nano Banana Pro is recommended for text-heavy images. Small text is still unreliable, and Google's own prompts often just add 'No text.'
findings.detail: API: 'Be clear about the text, the font style (descriptively), and the overall design. Use Gemini 3 Pro Image for professional asset production.' 'When generating text for an image, Gemini works best if you first generate the text and then ask for an image with the text.' DeepMind guide: 'Enclose your desired words in quotes... describe the typography style'. Nano Banana Pro tips limitation: 'Rendering small text, fine details, and producing accurate spellings may not work perfectly.' Google examples: 'Make the icons in a colorful and tactile 3D style. No text.' and 'In the style of bright colored Synthetic Cubism. No text.' The Gemini app says 'Redo with Pro' adds detail 'especially for images that use text rendering or for infographics'.

findings.claim: F24: Other documented limits: the model doesn't reliably produce the number of images you ask for, and it works best in a set list of languages that includes English and Vietnamese.
findings.detail: API Limitations: 'The model won't always follow the exact number of image outputs that the user explicitly asks for.' 'For best performance, use the following languages: EN, ar-EG, de-DE, es-MX, fr-FR, hi-IN, id-ID, it-IT, ja-JP, ko-KR, pt-BR, ru-RU, ua-UA, vi-VN, zh-CN.' Search grounding on 2.1 and 3.1 Flash does 'not support using real-world images of people from web search'. The DeepMind guide still suggests asking for 'three distinct variations' to compare options.

findings.claim: F25: Multi-turn chat is Google's recommended way to refine images, and 2.1 holds consistency across turns better. But long edit chats use more of the app allowance, and consistency across edits can still drift.
findings.detail: API: 'Multi-turn conversation is the recommended way to iterate on images.' Nano Banana 2.1 is described as improving 'multi-turn consistency'. The Gemini limits page rates 'Long chats with dynamic editing' as Medium cost and says: 'Start a new chat when you move to a new topic. This will help save usage'. Nano Banana Pro tips: 'While usually reliable, character consistency across edits may vary.'

findings.claim: F26: Google's Terms of Service (effective 30 July 2026) say Google does not claim ownership of content you generate. They forbid passing AI content off as human-made and using outputs to train AI models.
findings.detail: Quotes: 'Some of our services allow you to generate original content.' 'Google won't claim ownership over that content.' Prohibited: 'Misleading others into thinking that generative AI content was created by a human' and 'Using AI-generated content from our services to develop machine learning models or related AI technology'.

findings.claim: F27: Neither the Gemini app nor Flow docs grant an explicit commercial licence, and neither bans commercial use. Both point to the Terms of Service and the Prohibited Use Policy, and both make the user responsible for third-party rights, including rights to uploaded images.
findings.detail: Gemini app help: 'remember that you agreed to Google's Terms of Service, including the Prohibited Use Policy. Be sure not to violate others' copyright or privacy rights. Use your discretion before you rely on, publish, or use content that Gemini Apps generate.' The Flow FAQ question 'Can I use outputs of these tools for commercial purposes?' is answered only with: 'The Terms of Service govern how these tools may be used... Google won't claim ownership over that content'. The Prohibited Use Policy (last modified 2024-12-17) bans content that 'Violates the rights of others, including privacy and intellectual property rights' and 'Misrepresenting the provenance of generated content by claiming it was created solely by a human, in order to deceive.' API doc: 'Make sure you have the necessary rights to any images you upload.'

findings.claim: F28: Every Gemini app image carries an invisible SynthID watermark and C2PA Content Credentials. The visible watermark can be turned off in Settings > Media Watermark, except in India, South Korea and Vietnam, where only AI Ultra subscribers get the switch.
findings.detail: Quotes: 'If you are in India, South Korea, or Vietnam, you'll only see this setting if you have an AI Ultra subscription. Otherwise you'll automatically see visible watermarks applied to all visual media you create with Gemini Apps.' Web path: 'At the bottom left, click Settings > Media Watermark'. 'Images: Visible watermarks will appear on any newly generated images.' 'This setting only controls the visible watermark. It doesn't affect SynthID watermarks or Content Credentials'. 'All AI-generated media created or edited with Gemini Apps includes an invisible SynthID watermark.' 'Gemini Apps include Content Credentials (C2PA) metadata'. Third-party coverage dates the toggle to 2026-08-14.

findings.claim: F29: All Flow images carry SynthID. Flow has its own 'Visible watermarking' toggle, but in India, South Korea and Vietnam the visible watermark is forced on unless the user is on Google One AI Ultra 20x.
findings.detail: Quotes: 'All outputs generated in Google Flow using Veo, Omni, or Nano Banana include invisible SynthID watermarks.' 'You can control this with the "Visible watermarking" toggle in the drop-down menu under your profile picture.' 'A visible watermark will be applied automatically for users in India, South Korea, and Vietnam who are not on the Google One AI Ultra 20x Plan.' Flow's YouTube section says SynthID 'should not be tampered with or removed'. Note the difference: the Gemini app (F28) only says 'AI Ultra'.

findings.claim: F30: SUPERSEDED: under the November 2025 policy, free and Pro users always got the visible 'Gemini sparkle', and only Ultra subscribers and AI Studio were exempt.
findings.detail: Nano Banana Pro launch post: 'we will maintain a visible watermark (the Gemini sparkle) on images generated by free and Google AI Pro tier users' and Google will 'remove the visible watermark from images generated by Google AI Ultra subscribers' and in Google AI Studio. The August 2026 toggle (F28/F29) replaced this.

findings.claim: F31: YouTube requires an AI disclosure only for realistic AI content; non-realistic or animated AI imagery does not need one. YouTube may still auto-label videos that contain C2PA metadata or that its systems detect as AI, and C2PA-based labels cannot be removed.
findings.detail: Must disclose content that 'Generates a realistic scene that didn't actually occur', among others. 'Creators don't need to disclose non-realistic content that's made with AI'. Example: 'Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video'. Also exempt: 'Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic'. 'YouTube may automatically apply an AI label... for: ... Content that contains C2PA metadata; Content that our internal systems detect is Al generated or altered'. 'content containing C2PA metadata... can not be adjusted.' 'Disclosing AI content alone won't limit a video's audience or impact its eligibility to earn money.' Repeatedly failing to disclose can mean penalties, up to suspension from the Partner Program.

findings.claim: F32: YouTube's monetisation rules allow AI visuals of characters and stories you invent. They demonetise templated or mass-produced AI content and image slideshows with little narrative, and they demonetise AI personas posing as human experts on finance and other sensitive topics.
findings.detail: Not monetisable: 'Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value'; 'AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator's original, authentic insights or perspective'; 'Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome'. Allowed: 'using AI to visualize a unique character and narrative you invented'; 'Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes'. AI personas section: channels 'that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics... a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances' cannot monetise. Example: 'AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance'. The repetitious-to-inauthentic rename was announced 2025-07-15; the AI-persona section carries no date.

findings.claim: F33: Under US Copyright Office guidance, a prompt alone does not make you the author of an AI image. Raw outputs have little copyright protection; protection comes from human selection, arrangement or modification.
findings.detail: Copyright and AI Part 2 report (US government; labelled third_party here because it is not Google): AI outputs can be protected only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements, which does not include 'the mere provision of prompts'. Repeatedly revising prompts does not change this. This is policy analysis, not binding law.

findings.claim: F34: Vietnam's AI Law (Law No. 134/2025/QH15) took effect on 1 March 2026 and requires AI content to be labelled. A draft decree would set watermark and metadata rules and ban removing labels. This probably explains why Google forces visible watermarks in Vietnam.
findings.detail: Law-firm summaries: the law took effect 1 March 2026. AI-generated audio, image and video must be marked in a visible and/or machine-readable form. The draft labelling decree (watermark plus metadata for images; no removing or interfering with labels) was not confirmed final in what I found. Not legal advice; it matters only if the owner is physically in Vietnam.

findings.claim: F35: Google AI Studio is a manual fallback that exposes the model's ratio and size controls, but using the newer image models there needs a paid API key.
findings.detail: 'Build with Nano Banana 2' post: 'A paid api key is required to use the model on Google AI Studio.' The API config (F11) shows aspect_ratio and image_size exist. In Nov 2025 Google removed the visible watermark in AI Studio (F30). I did not verify AI Studio's current UI for Nano Banana 2.1.

findings.claim: F36: Gemini now has 'Skills': saved instructions that run automatically on matching prompts. They replace Gems. It is not documented whether they apply to image generation.
findings.detail: Release note 2026-09-30, 'Skills in Gemini': Skills are reusable instructions built from your chats that run automatically on matching prompts. They can be combined, they replace Gems (Gems migrate automatically), and they are 18+ at launch. Nothing says whether a Skill can carry a reference image or affects image requests.

implications: I1 Model check (F1, F3, F4, F7, F15): start every copy-paste prompt pack with an owner checklist. Gemini app: paid plan, chat model set to Fast/Thinking/Pro, never Flash-Lite. Flow: choose 'Nano Banana 2.1' or 'Nano Banana Pro' by hand. Never use Nano Banana 2 Lite (Flow's free default, and the Gemini fallback after a usage cap) for any shot that relies on the reference sheet, because Google says it 'isn't designed for multiple image references or for multiple edits'. If Gemini reports a limit or a switch to Flash-Lite, stop and wait for the 5-hour refresh.

I2 Resolution check (F5, F12): production frames must be 2K downloads ('Download full size' on a paid plan; expect 2752x1536). A free 1K frame (1376x768) needs about 1.9x upscaling for 1440p and should be rejected. Our importer should flag any image under 2560x1440 and any ratio that is not about 1.79.

I3 Remotion fit (F12): treat Nano Banana's '16:9' as 2752x1536 (43:24). Scale to 1440 px high (2580 wide) and centre-crop 10 px per side, i.e. cover fit with no letterbox. Every scene prompt should add 'keep all characters and key objects well inside the frame' so the crop never cuts faces or hands.

I4 Aspect ratio wording (F11, F13, F14): end every image prompt with the same line: 'Format: widescreen 16:9 landscape image (aspect ratio 16:9).' Generate the master reference sheet itself in 16:9, because the API defaults to the input image's size. In Flow, also set Image > aspect ratio 16:9 in the UI. Check the pixel size of each download.

I5 Reference budget (F6, F7, F8): every scene prompt attaches Image 1 = the script's master character sheet, plus at most 3 extra images (a per-character close-up, a location or a prop). That keeps us within 4 character-identity images for Nano Banana 2.1/2 and well under the app's 10-file cap. Draw at most 4 named characters in one frame. If a shot needs 5, split it or use Redo with Pro (5 character references). This takes the lower figure where Google's sources conflict.

I6 Reference labels (F9, F21): every scene prompt opens with a REFERENCES block that lists each attachment in upload order with exactly one job. Example: 'Image 1 = CHARACTER SHEET: use only for each character's identity, body proportions, outfit colours and drawing style. Image 2 = LOCATION: use only for the room layout.' Characters are always called by the exact name printed on the sheet, spelled the same way, and attachments go in the same order every time.

I7 Anti-copy clause (F10, F22): Nano Banana 2.1 can keep 'structural alignment' and 'persistent subject pose' from an input image. So every scene prompt must say: 'Do not reproduce the sheet's layout, plain background, name labels or poses; draw a new scene.' Then describe each character's pose in words. Never write only 'use pose 3 from the sheet'.

I8 Master sheet layout (F7, F8, F10, F22, F23): one 16:9 image at 2K per script on a plain flat light background. Each character gets one row: a full-body neutral front view first, then every pose and expression the script uses, all at the same scale, with no overlaps and generous gaps. Above each row, print the character's name once in large bold capitals (one short word); the sheet has no other text, because small text renders badly. Give every character a unique high-contrast outfit colour so identity never depends on left/right position. If a script has more than about 4 characters or about 24 figures in total, keep this sheet as the overview and also make one sheet per character, because figures shrink and Google only guarantees 4-5 consistent characters.

I9 Building the sheet (F21, F22, F25): (1) A text-only prompt makes a lineup of all characters (front view) in the locked style. (2) Attach the lineup as Image 1 and ask for the full pose sheet; this follows Google's 360-view advice to 'include previously generated images in subsequent prompts'. (3) Fix defects with Google's edit template: 'Using the provided image, change only [X] to [Y]. Keep everything else in the image exactly the same, preserving the original style, lighting, and composition.' (4) Freeze the result as sheet_vN.png, write the version into the script's prompt file, and never regenerate it mid-video.

I10 Style lock without the third-party image (F26, F27, F20): never upload the third-party model sheet and never name its brand, studio or artist. Google requires rights to anything uploaded, and the Prohibited Use Policy bans IP violations. Instead, turn its generic traits into one fixed STYLE block using Google's illustration template ('A [style] of [subject]... The design features [bold outlines, flat colour, etc.] and [colour/background]'). Paste that block word-for-word into every character, sheet and scene prompt. Our own approved sheet is the only visual style reference.

I11 Phrasing (F19, F23): describe what should be in the scene ('plain empty beige wall', 'clear wooden desk') instead of listing 'no X', per Google's 'semantic negative prompts' advice. Keep exactly one short exclusion line, the kind Google's own examples use: 'No text, letters, numbers, logos, captions or speech bubbles in the image.' All on-screen text and figures are added in Remotion.

I12 Identity cards (F9, F19, F21): for each character in a frame, also paste the same one-line identity card: name plus 4-5 fixed traits (hair, skin tone, body shape, outfit colours, one signature item). The text must be identical across every prompt in the project; this is Google's 'describe critical details in great detail' advice applied to characters.

I13 Scene prompt order (F10, F19, F20): REFERENCES, then STYLE block, then characters (identity card + pose + expression), then action, then setting, then composition/camera (shot size and angle; place characters with foreground/background and distinctive props, not left/right alone), then the Format line, then the exclusion line. For complex scenes use 'First... Then... Finally...'. Ancient-life channel: add 'Ensure historical accuracy for [period, region]' plus the specific materials, clothing and tools from our research, then check the output.

I14 One image per prompt (F22, F24): ask for exactly one image per prompt. If a sequence is truly needed, use Google's wording 'Generate N images one at a time, each a separate 16:9 output' and expect the count to vary.

I15 Chat habits (F4, F25): one chat per scene group of about 5-8 frames. Re-attach the sheet in every prompt instead of relying on chat memory. Use follow-up turns only for local fixes ('change only...'). Start a new chat for the next group to save usage and stop errors carrying over.

I16 Frames with text (F1, F23): avoid text inside images. If it is unavoidable, generate with Nano Banana 2.1, then 'Redo with Pro', with the exact words in quotes, a described font, 6 words or fewer, set large.

I17 Flow route (F14-F17): in Flow, create one Character per recurring cast member from 1-2 crops of the master sheet (front view plus the most-used pose) and prompt with @Name. Add the full sheet via 'Add to Prompt'. Set Image to 16:9, 1-2 outputs, model Nano Banana 2.1 or Pro. Check the credit cost in Settings, and confirm the downloaded image size before using Flow for production frames.

I18 Watermarks (F28, F29, F34): before each session, check Gemini Settings > Media Watermark and Flow profile menu > Visible watermarking; the switch only affects newly generated images. If the owner is physically in Vietnam (or India/South Korea), removing the visible mark needs AI Ultra in Gemini or Ultra 20x in Flow. Do not crop or cover a forced watermark until Vietnam's labelling rules are checked, and never try to strip SynthID or C2PA.

I19 YouTube safety (F31, F32): keep the style clearly illustrated and non-photorealistic. That makes frames 'non-realistic' AI content needing no disclosure, and avoids realistic 'scene that didn't occur' reconstructions for the ancient channel. If any frame is realistic, tick 'AI use: Yes'. In The Median Worker, the recurring cast must be everyday people living through situations, never an AI 'host' or 'expert' giving money advice (YouTube's AI-persona rule). Vary scenes, angles and settings between videos so the channel doesn't look templated.

I20 Licence records (F26, F27, F33): monetised use fits the Terms (Google claims no ownership), but there is no explicit commercial grant. Keep a log per image: tool, model, date, prompt, sheet version. Never describe the images as hand-drawn, and never upload third-party art, stock photos or photos of real people. Assume raw frames are barely protectable; the script and edit carry the originality.
I21 Language (F24): write the copy-paste prompts in English (supported, as is vi-VN). Keep Vietnamese notes for the owner outside the prompt block so they are not pasted into the generator.

I22 Skills, optional (F36): the STYLE and REFERENCES rules could be saved as a Gemini Skill to reduce paste mistakes. Still include the full blocks in every prompt until a test shows Skills affect image generation.

I23 Exception path (F11, F35): if the Gemini app won't reliably give 16:9 at 2K, Google AI Studio exposes aspect ratio and size settings, but it needs a paid API key/billing. Keep it as an exception, not the default workflow.
open_questions: Which Gemini app mode sends paid users to Nano Banana 2.1, and has the staged rollout (started 2026-10-06) reached the owner's account? The help center still says Nano Banana 2 for Flash/Pro.

Does the Gemini app reliably follow '16:9' written in the prompt with Nano Banana 2 and 2.1? There is no official statement and no in-app selector is documented; the 'unreliable' reports are from 2025. Test 3-5 prompts and check the pixel sizes.

What exact pixel size does 'Download full size' give for a 16:9 image at 2K in the Gemini app? The API table says 2752x1536, unverified for the app. Also, the overview page lists '2K resolution' for free Nano Banana 2 while the help center says free downloads are 1K.
When several images with different aspect ratios are attached and the prompt doesn't settle it, which one sets the output size? The API only says output 'matches... your input image'.

Does one composite sheet with many characters and poses keep identity as well as separate per-character images? Does the '4 character images' limit count images or characters inside an image? Neither is documented; an A/B test is needed.
Is Nano Banana 2.1 good for 4 or 5 consistent characters, and 10 or 14 objects? The API doc (2026-10-09) and the marketing pages disagree.

Flow, still images: which download resolutions exist (1K/2K/4K, upscale?), how many credits each model costs per image, how many image ingredients one prompt allows, and whether a paid plan is strictly required (the help pages conflict). Also, does the 'By default... Nano Banana Pro' sentence apply only to Ultra?
If an attached reference image carries a visible watermark, does the model copy that mark into new images? Not documented.
Does 'Redo with Pro' reuse the same attached reference images and prompt as the original generation? Not documented.
Do Gemini Skills apply to image-generation requests, and can a Skill include a reference image?
Can YouTube's 'internal systems detect' AI label pick up SynthID in a Remotion-rendered MP4 built from Gemini stills? Our render probably drops the images' C2PA metadata (my inference, unverified).
Is the owner physically in Vietnam? If so, has the AI-labelling decree under Law 134/2025/QH15 been finalised, and would it forbid cropping or covering the forced visible watermark?
After the May 2026 switch to compute-based limits, roughly how many 2K Nano Banana 2.1 images fit into one 5-hour window on Plus, Pro and Ultra? Google publishes no numbers.

findings.claim: Google's current image models accept different numbers of character references. Nano Banana 2.1 takes up to 4 character images and 10 object images. Nano Banana Pro takes up to 5 characters, 6 objects and 3 style references. Nano Banana 2 Lite takes object images only. The total is capped at 14 images.
findings.detail: Gemini API image-generation page, last updated 2026-10-09. It lists Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) as 'the primary high-efficiency workhorse model', Nano Banana 2 (gemini-3.1-flash-image) as the previous generation, Nano Banana 2 Lite (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Nano Banana Pro (gemini-3-pro-image). Quote: 'Nano Banana models allow you to mix up to 14 reference images.' The table for 2.1 and 3.1 Flash Image says 'Up to 10 images of objects with high-fidelity' and 'Up to 4 images of characters to maintain character consistency', with style 'N/A'. For 3 Pro Image it says 'Up to 6 images of objects', 'Up to 5 images of characters' and 'Up to 3 images to be used as style references'. The Limitations section adds: 'gemini-nano-banana-2.1 and gemini-3.1-flash-image support character resemblance of up to 4 characters and the fidelity of up to 10 objects in a single workflow.' Launch press in Feb 2026 said Nano Banana 2 handled 5 characters and 14 objects. The current page says 4 and 10.

findings.claim: Google's official advice for multi-angle views: generate the character one angle at a time, attach earlier outputs to later prompts, and attach a picture of the pose when the pose is complex.
findings.detail: Section '7. Character consistency: 360 view': 'You can generate 360-degree views of a character by iteratively prompting for different angles. For best results, include previously generated images in subsequent prompts to maintain consistency. For complex poses, include a reference image of the selected pose.' Template: 'A studio portrait of [person] against [background], [looking forward/in profile looking right/etc.]'. Example: 'A studio portrait of this man against white, in profile looking right'.

findings.claim: Google's best practices are: be very specific, give the image's purpose, iterate in conversation, give step-by-step instructions, and describe what you want instead of writing 'no X' (what Google calls 'semantic negative prompts'). Google also warns that the model does not always produce the exact number of things you ask for.
findings.detail: Quote: 'Use "semantic negative prompts": Instead of saying "no cars," describe the intended scene positively: "an empty, deserted street with no signs of traffic."' Its iteration example is 'Keep everything the same, but change the character's expression to be more serious.' Quote: 'Multi-turn conversation is the recommended way to iterate on images.' Limitations: 'The model won't always follow the exact number of image outputs that the user explicitly asks for.' The languages listed for best performance include EN and vi-VN.

findings.claim: Google's official prompt templates cover style and locked edits. For a consistent style, name the visual details (outlines, colours) and the background. For an edit, say what changes and that everything else stays exactly the same. Google also says you must have rights to the images you upload.
findings.detail: Stylized illustrations section: 'Be specific about the visual detail (bold lines, colors, etc.) for consistent results.' Template: 'The design features [visual qualities, e.g., bold outlines, cel-shading, etc.] and [color/background preference].' The sample prompt ends with 'The background must be white.' Inpainting template: 'Using the provided image, change only the [specific element] to [new element/description]. Keep everything else in the image exactly the same, preserving the original style, lighting, and composition.' Detail-preservation template: 'Ensure that the features of [element from image 1] remain completely unchanged.' Editing section: 'Make sure you have the necessary rights to any images you upload.'

findings.claim: Output aspect ratio follows the attached image unless you set it. At 16:9, Nano Banana 2.1 and Pro render 1376x768 at 1K, 2752x1536 at 2K and 5504x3072 at 4K.
findings.detail: Quote: 'By default, the model matches the output image size to that of your input image, or otherwise generates 1:1 squares.' The size tables give 16:9 as 1376x768 / 2752x1536 / 5504x3072 for Nano Banana 2.1 and for the Pro table. Google's consistent-imagery notebook adds that when the ratio is omitted, Gemini uses the ratio of the input image, 'the last one if multiple are provided'. The channel's 2560x1440 frame is larger than 1K and smaller than 2K.

findings.claim: Nano Banana 2 Lite is not designed for work with reference images or repeated edits. It is the model the Gemini app uses when set to Flash-Lite, and the no-charge default model in Flow.
findings.detail: Gemini Apps Help on Nano Banana 2 Lite: 'This option is used when the Gemini model is set to Flash-Lite' and 'It isn't designed for multiple image references or for multiple edits.' On Nano Banana 2: 'This option is selected when you make an image request with the Gemini model set to Flash or Pro.' The API page says Lite is 'Not optimized for multiple reference inputs or multi-turn sequential editing.' The Flow models page (support.google.com/flow/answer/16352836) says Nano Banana 2 Lite 'is the default model available at no charge', Nano Banana Pro 'is the default model for Google AI Ultra subscribers', and Nano Banana 2.1 is 'The standard model for fast, high-quality image generation and editing.'

findings.claim: In the Gemini app, downloads are 2K only with a paid Google AI plan (1K otherwise), and one prompt can carry up to 10 files.
findings.detail: Gemini Apps Help: 'Download images at at 2K resolution with a Google AI plan or at 1K without an AI plan.' AI-plan users can redo an image with Nano Banana Pro from the three-dot menu. The upload help (support.google.com/gemini/answer/14903178) says: 'Up to 10 files (subject to availability) can be uploaded in the same prompt.' The help page still names Nano Banana 2, while the gemini.google overview page already lists Nano Banana 2.1 features. DeepMind's prompt guide calls the 2K/4K choice an in-product 'upscale'.

findings.claim: In Google Flow you set the model, aspect ratio and number of outputs for each prompt. You can reference an image with 'Add to Prompt' or a character with '@' plus its name, and edits are saved to the image's version history.
findings.detail: Flow Help, 'Create & edit images in Google Flow': select Image, then set the aspect ratio, number of outputs and model. The page says 'By default, Google Flow sets the model to Nano Banana Pro', but the models page shows the default depends on plan. To reference an image, choose More > Add to Prompt; for characters, 'type @ followed by the character name'. 'Edits are automatically saved to the asset's stack', and the History panel keeps earlier versions. No limit on reference images and no resolution options are documented. The Feb 25, 2026 relaunch added a lasso tool for editing selected areas (The Decoder).

findings.claim: Flow's official tips for reference images: put subjects on a plain or segmented background, keep the same look across all reference images, and write prompts that point to the references without contradicting them.
findings.detail: Flow Help, 'Create videos in Google Flow': 'For the best results, provide subject or product references on a plain or segmented background.' 'A consistent look and feel across all your ingredient images helps the model blend them more effectively.' The text prompt 'should complement, not contradict, your visual inputs.' Refer to the frames or ingredients you provided in the prompt, and reuse the same character and object images from clip to clip. These tips are written for video ingredients in the same Flow workspace, so they apply to still images only by analogy.

findings.claim: Google's official notebook on consistent images shows the workflow: make a labelled character sheet on a pure white background, then attach it as Image 1 to every scene prompt. Details that the sheet or prompt leaves open come out differently on each run.
findings.detail: GoogleCloudPlatform notebook by Laurent Picard (Google), linked from codelabs.developers.google.com/gemini-consistent-imagery-notebook; last commit 2026-08-31. Sheet prompt lines: 'Scene: Character sheet of the robot, based on the provided image.' 'Setting: Isolated on a pure white background, razor-sharp focus, vibrant saturated colors, bright studio lighting.' 'Left Side: Straight-on front view...' 'Right Side: Straight-on back view...' 'Text: Small sans-serif text. Centered at the top, a caption ROBOT CHARACTER SHEET. At the bottom, label the left side FRONT VIEW and the right side BACK VIEW.' Notes: everything visible in the reference stays consistent, but the loosely described backpack differs between runs, and 'In a real production pipeline, we would likely make it part of a separate accessory sheet.' The first scene 'will have a cascading effect that defines the overall look of our story.' Prompts and source image IDs are saved in the PNG metadata.

findings.claim: The same notebook shows four rules for using a sheet. Number each attached image and its role, because a sheet contains several copies of the character. Say explicitly which props are dropped. Expect lighting and background to carry over from an attached previous scene. Add left and right side views to the sheet so the character can face either way.
findings.detail: Scene prompts start 'Image 1: Reference robot character sheet.' and 'Image 2: Previous scene.' Note: 'Without them, the robot could refer to any of the three robots in the input images (two in the character sheet, one in the previous scene)... we can be more specific with the [entity] from image [number].' Quote: 'The no longer holding the map instruction prevents the model from carrying it over.' Without 'Remove the ice picks' the result would be random. Quote: 'Since we didn't provide lighting details, the light source, quality, and direction are preserved from the previous scene.' Quote: 'getting it to consistently walk from left to right is tricky. Adding left and right views to the character sheet should fix this.' A lock phrase used: 'Its face and hands are unchanged.' Both imperative and descriptive prompts worked.

findings.claim: DeepMind's prompt guide says to give each character a distinct name with clear reference images, put exact text in quotes, and state the aspect ratio. It describes 2K and 4K in Google's apps as an upscale.
findings.detail: Quote: 'Upload clear reference images, and assign a distinct name to each character or object in your prompt.' Quote: 'Prompt for your desired aspect ratio (like 4:3, 1:1, or 9:16) and describe the image format you need.' Quote: 'Look for the in-product resolution dropdowns to upscale to 2K or 4K.' Quote: 'Enclose your desired words in quotes (e.g., Happy Birthday).' Prompt components: Style, Subject, Setting, Action, Composition. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Google Cloud's prompting guide gives a formula for reference prompts: [Reference images] + [Relationship instruction] + [New scenario]. For edits, state exactly what stays the same, and phrase requests positively.
findings.detail: 'The ultimate Nano Banana prompting guide', Google Cloud Blog, Mar 6, 2026 (K. Davaajav, H. Chinoy). It gives the formula above. Quote: 'Editing requires a different mindset than generating... your prompt needs to focus on what is changing and what is staying the same.' Quote: 'Be explicit about what to keep exactly the same.' Quote: 'Use positive framing: Describe what you want, not what you don't want (e.g. empty street instead of no cars).' Quote: 'You can mix up to 14 reference object images in a single prompt.' It has no guidance on character sheets.

findings.claim: Google's Developers Blog: if a character drifts after many edits, start a new conversation with a detailed description. Ask for a white background explicitly when you need one.
findings.detail: 'How to prompt Gemini 2.5 Flash Image Generation for the best results', Aug 28, 2025 (Philipp Schmid, Logan Kilpatrick, Alisa Fortin). Quote: '...you can restart a new conversation with a detailed description to retain consistency.' Quote: 'remember to request a white background if you need one.' It says character consistency 'sometimes needs refinement through follow-up prompts'. It was written for the 2025 model and may be outdated, although the 2026 model cards still list consistency drift as a limitation.

findings.claim: Google says neither style nor character consistency is guaranteed: 'character consistency across edits may vary'. Google also recommends stating the role of each attached image.
findings.detail: blog.google, '7 tips to get the most out of Nano Banana Pro' (Nov 20, 2025, B. Alessio): 'character consistency across edits may vary.' It advises defining each image's role, for example one for pose and another for art style, and says you can blend 'up to 6 to 14 (input number varies by surface)' images. The earlier tips post (Aug 26, 2025) says 'the model's stylization can sometimes be inconsistent or produce unexpected results' and 'While the model excels at character consistency, it may not always get it right.' Both posts cover older models and may be outdated.

findings.claim: DeepMind lists small faces, spelling and fine detail as weak points of Nano Banana Pro. It says blending several images or making complex edits can produce artifacts, and that the model keeps up to five characters consistent.
findings.detail: Nano Banana Pro page: 'it can still struggle with small faces, accurate spelling, and fine details in images.' Quote: 'blending multiple images may sometimes produce unnatural results, visual artifacts, or disjointed scenes.' Quote: 'Maintain the consistency and resemblance of up to five characters and the fidelity of up to fourteen objects in a single workflow.' Quote: 'The model excels at character consistency, but it may not always get it right.'

findings.claim: Google's model cards list the same known failures for Pro, 2 and 2.1: small text is blurry at 1K, the character is not always identical to the reference, parts of the input image are sometimes pasted into the output, left and right get confused, and 2.1 sometimes keeps the pose of the input image.
findings.detail: Nano Banana 2.1 model card, published 6 Oct 2026: 'Poor text rendering in small text (often blurry in 1k model)'; 'Character consistency is not always perfect between input images and generated output image'; 'Occasional confusion around spatial localisation (e.g. left/right etc.)'; 'rare instances of persistent subject pose, where structural alignment from the input image is retained'. The Gemini 3 Pro Image card (Nov 2025) and the 3.1 Flash Image card (Feb 2026) also list: 'When editing images: infrequent copying/pasting from user's input image to generated image'.

findings.claim: In Google's own human ratings, Nano Banana 2.1 with thinking scores clearly above Nano Banana Pro for keeping several characters consistent and for stylization.
findings.detail: Nano Banana 2.1 model card, Elo scores from side-by-side human evaluation. Multi-character consistency: 1106 for 2.1 with thinking, 1068 for 2.1 without, 1011 for 3 Pro Image, 978 for 3.1 Flash Image. Single character: 1028 / 1021 / 991 / 981. Stylization: 1062 / 1036 / 990 / 991. In the API, 2.1's thinking level can be minimal, medium or high (default medium). These are Google's own evaluations and have not been replicated independently.

findings.claim: Images made in the Gemini app on free and Google AI Pro accounts carry a visible Gemini sparkle watermark. Ultra subscribers' images do not. This is the policy announced in Nov 2025.
findings.detail: blog.google, 'Introducing Nano Banana Pro' (Nov 20, 2025): 'we will maintain a visible watermark (the Gemini sparkle) on images generated by free and Google AI Pro tier users' and 'we will remove the visible watermark from images generated by Google AI Ultra subscribers' (also removed in Google AI Studio). Flow Help says a visible watermark 'can be added to generated images and videos'. A vendor blog claims a settings toggle since Aug 2026, which I could not confirm. The policy may be outdated.

findings.claim: A Google developer advocate's guide says: fix an almost-right image with a targeted edit instead of regenerating ('Edit, Don't Re-roll'), lock identity to a numbered image, and state one style that applies to all images.
findings.detail: Guillaume Vernade (Senior Developer Advocate, Google AI), posted on dev.to/googleai Nov 27, 2025 and edited Jan 2026. Identity-lock wording: 'Keep the person's facial features exactly the same as Image 1', with pose or emotion changes asked for in a separate sentence. Images are referred to by number and given roles. Style example: a 'Modern Minimalist style' applied 'across ALL images'. A 3x3 sprite grid is shown as possible. The post predates Nano Banana 2 and 2.1.

findings.claim: Users report that chaining edits wears the image down: after 5 to 10 edits, each made on the previous output, sharpness drops and colours and structure distort.
findings.detail: Post on Google's AI developer forum, July 15, 2026, about gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview: '5-10 iterative re-edits, each using the previous output as the new base image' produce artifacts that 'compound with each pass'. Google did not reply. A similar Adobe Community thread (July 9, 2026) about Gemini 3.1 inside Firefly says 'The image quality of each edit degrades compared with last' and 'the entire image degrades, not just the character'.

findings.claim: A practitioner found that the character changed too much unless each prompt listed what must stay the same. The chat sometimes went back to an earlier image, and re-uploading the chosen image as a reference stopped the drift.
findings.detail: Christy Tucker, Oct 21, 2025, using the original Nano Banana, so this may be outdated. Working prompt: 'Keep the character details the same (hair, glasses, blouse, etc.) but change her expression to ...'. Makeup and skin tone shifted, and a notebook prop disappeared between images. In scenes with two characters, changing the camera angle mostly failed; only zooming out worked.

findings.claim: One user found that Nano Banana 2 'cleans up' deliberately crude drawings unless told not to. Banning gradients, 3D shading and digital touch-ups, and requiring the original rough lines, kept the style. In a long chat the drawings drifted cleaner, and a new chat fixed it.
findings.detail: Kaga Hajime, note.com, Mar 1, 2026, using one hand-drawn reference on white. Some sitting, walking and running poses came out 'a bit too smart-looking' until that look was banned in the prompt. Hair colour drifted, and the eyes needed fixing by hand. In a long chat the model pulled in earlier material. Key advice: tell the AI 'Don't make it look pretty on your own.'

findings.claim: A vendor's stick-figure test (Oct 2026): a sheet plus a fixed 'lock' sentence and style line in every prompt kept the figure consistent. 'Hands with no fingers' came out as solid mitten hands. A one-sided cap brim flipped with the facing direction. Nano Banana 2 Lite drifted in style in 4 of 10 shots and added numerals despite 'no numbers'.
findings.detail: BulkImagen Team, Oct 17, 2026; vendor content promoting its own bulk tool. The sheet prompt asked for a round white head with a thick black outline, two dot eyes, a small smile, single thick black limbs, 'simple hands with no fingers', an off-white paper background and no text. The generated sheet then became the reference. Each shot prompt was 'Shot NN' plus a camera direction, the lock sentence 'the stick figure from the reference image, kept exactly as it is' with the fixed traits listed, the style line 'simple hand-drawn black marker line art on an off-white paper background', and 'no text, no letters, no numbers, no logos'. Nano Banana 2 kept the style. Props were sometimes simplified, and objects nobody asked for appeared. With only 10 shots, the authors call the drift figure 'a warning, not a rate'.

findings.claim: Imitation xkcd comics from Gemini 3 Pro Image had perfectly geometric circle heads instead of hand-drawn loops, and mixed digital fonts with hand lettering.
findings.detail: danprice.ai, Dec 2, 2025: mixed fonts were the 'single most reliable indicator' that a strip was fake, and heads were 'mathematically perfect circles'. This was an older model. It matters for us because sheet labels may come out in mixed lettering styles.

findings.claim: Storyboard advice from a vendor: generate 5 to 10 frames per location as a batch and review them in order, refresh the reference image for long sequences, state where each character stands, avoid extreme angles, and keep per-shot character descriptions short.
findings.detail: Flowith blog (vendor), Mar 12, 2026. Example position line: 'Character A (Maya) stands on the left, Character B (Ruiz) sits on the right.' Failures it lists: prompts without a reference image drift, changing style mid-sequence breaks consistency, extreme angles and foreshortening hurt, long descriptions in every prompt reduce consistency, and small details such as jewellery vary. Its '90%+' consistency claim is unverified.

findings.claim: Some practitioners say a sheet generated in one shot can merge views, get the small expression heads wrong and invent back views. They generate each view separately and assemble the sheet by hand.
findings.detail: AI Photo Generator blog (vendor), Jul 7, 2026: models 'merge views, mismatch expression miniatures, and invent back views'; it recommends locking the front view first and compositing the rest in an editor. Our Code World (Aug 26, 2026): 'Full-body compositions allocate fewer pixels to the face, making small identity details harder to preserve' and 'Some models mirror images', so check one-sided details. Neither source ran controlled tests.

findings.claim: Traditional animation practice for comparing characters: draw every character head to toe in a relaxed stance side by side, use the main character's height as the measuring stick, label each figure with its name, keep silhouettes distinct, and use 5 to 7 expressions per character.
findings.detail: Charles Merritt Houghton, Nov 2024 (articles on comparison charts and design sheets). Quote: 'Draw each character from head to toe in a relaxed stance, side by side.' Quote: 'Label each silhouette with the character's name.' Quote: 'Mark each character's height, shoulder width, or distinctive features.' Quote: 'Whenever characters appear together, consult the comparison sheet.' Quote: 'A set of five to seven expressions.' This is not specific to AI.

findings.claim: A green-screen recipe for Nano Banana Pro cut-outs: ask for a flat #00FF00 background, keep green out of the subject, remove a narrow range of green, then clean the edges. The author prefers this to AI background removal.
findings.detail: Philipp Schmid's personal blog, Jan 19, 2026; he co-wrote Google's Aug 2025 prompting guide. Prompt text: 'Solid, flat, uniform chromakey green color. Use EXACTLY hex color #00FF00 (RGB 0, 255, 0).' Quote: 'The subject itself should NOT contain any green colors'. If the subject needs green, use dark forest green or teal. An optional 2-3 px white outline 'prevents color bleeding'. Removal settings: hue 120 plus or minus 25, saturation at least 75, value at least 70, mask widened by 2 px, edge threshold 64. He calls AI background removal 'Slower and more expensive' with edges that are 'hit or miss'. A white background was not tested.

findings.claim: The model returns a near-green such as #05F904, not exact #00FF00, so cut-out scripts should sample the background colour from the image corners and remove green spill from the edges.
findings.detail: README of the GitHub tool kingbootoshi/nano-banana-2-skill: 'The key color is auto-detected from corner pixels', because the AI 'generates near-green like #05F904, not exact #00FF00'. It uses FFmpeg colorkey plus despill to avoid a 'green fringe'. This also shows that hex colours in prompts are only approximate.

findings.claim: Nano Banana images have no transparency channel. Asking for a 'transparent' background gives a painted checkerboard or a plain backdrop. Recovering soft edges from a white and a black version works only if the two images line up pixel for pixel.
findings.detail: Transparify (vendor), Jun 7, 2026: 'Google's image models output flat RGB pixels with no alpha channel'. A painted checkerboard is made of 'real, opaque pixels, not transparency', so leave the word 'transparent' out of prompts. To get the black version, edit the white render rather than generating again, because a fresh render 'may shift slightly and introduce artifacts'. Green is suggested as a fallback. A second vendor, image-editor-ai.online (Sep 13, 2026), gives prompts for white, light grey and #00FF00 backdrops and notes that hair, fur and translucent edges rarely cut cleanly.

findings.claim: The basic rule of colour keying is that the subject must not contain the background colour. Green and blue are used because they differ from skin tones, colour can spill onto edges, any flat distinct colour works, and magenta #FF00FF is a classic digital key colour.
findings.detail: Wikipedia, 'Chroma key'. Quote: 'No part of the subject being filmed or photographed may duplicate the colour used as the backing.' Quote: 'green and blue backgrounds... differ most distinctly in hue from any human skin colour.' It describes spill. Quote: 'chroma keying can be done with backgrounds of any colour that are uniform and distinct.' It mentions 'full-intensity magenta colour #FF00FF in digital colour images to encode (1-bit) transparency'.

findings.claim: Research shows that naming what to leave out can backfire: diffusion image models such as Stable Diffusion and DALL-E 3 often draw the very thing the prompt says to omit.
findings.detail: Hwang, Kim and Lee, 'Do not think about pink elephant!' (CVPR 2024 workshop), which calls it the 'white bear phenomenon'. Their defences describe alternative concepts instead of negating. Gemini image models were not tested. The finding supports Google's own advice to phrase requests positively.

findings.claim: A creator's Flow workflow: make the character sheet at 16:9, generate two versions and pick one, use 'add to prompt', and upload both sheets together when a scene has two characters.
findings.detail: Summary on lilys.ai of the AI Video School YouTube video 'Consistent Character Sheets in Nano Banana' (Jan 23, 2026). The creator says 16:9 'works better' for sheets and checks fidelity by spinning the character in a video.

findings.claim: When Nano Banana 2 launched (Feb 26, 2026), it replaced Nano Banana Pro in all Gemini app modes. Pro stayed available to Pro and Ultra subscribers through regenerate. At launch Google claimed five characters and 14 objects; the current API page says 4 and 10.
findings.detail: 9to5Google, Feb 26, 2026: 'character resemblance of up to five characters and the fidelity of up to 14 objects in a single workflow'. It was the default image model in Flow at launch. Pro access: 'by regenerating images via the three-dot menu'. The current API page (Oct 2026) gives 4 characters and 10 objects for 2.1 and 3.1 Flash Image, so treat 4 as the safe limit.

findings.claim: A practitioner's reference-sheet layout (Apr 2026): full-body front, side and back views on the left; six head angles and six detail close-ups on the right; a white background; and the wording 'Same character. Same clothes. Same height.'
findings.detail: pIXELsHAM, Apr 18, 2026. The sheet was made in Nano Banana and used as a reference in a video model. Quotes: 'White background. Clean. Minimalist.' and 'No fancy backgrounds', 'No dramatic lighting'. No tested limit on figure count.

implications: Model choice: make every reference-based image (sheet, scene, cut-out) with Nano Banana 2.1. In Flow, select it by hand because the free default is 2 Lite. In the Gemini app, use any model except Flash-Lite. Use Nano Banana Pro only when one image must hold 5 named characters or needs dedicated style references. Never use 2 Lite with a reference sheet. Basis: API model list, Gemini and Flow help pages, the 2.1 model card scores, and the vendor test where Lite drifted in style.

Style block: keep one STYLE BLOCK per channel as a versioned text file and paste it unchanged into every prompt. Build it from the extracted traits, described positively: a plain white circular head with a thick black outline; a face made only of two small solid black dot eyes and one simple line mouth, with short eyebrow strokes only when an expression needs them; neck and arms as single thick black lines; small white oval mitten hands outlined in black; flat, muted earth-tone clothing and props with light texture and minimal soft shading; one uniform outline weight; a plain background. End with one short 'Never add' line: nose, ears, hair, fingers, pupils or irises, skin colour on the head, gradients, 3D or photo look. Basis: Google's advice to phrase positively and name visual details, plus the reports of models polishing simple styles and adding numerals despite 'no numbers'.

Third-party sheet: never attach the third-party sheet, and never copy its title or brand words into any prompt. Google requires rights to uploaded images. Its traits live only as text in the STYLE BLOCK, and our own approved sheet is the only image we use as a reference.

Character card: keep one card per character and reuse it word for word. It holds a unique one-word NAME (also the sheet label), height in head-units relative to the main character, each clothing item with its colour, one distinctive silhouette accessory, and the side of any one-sided item (stated from the character's own left or right). Every head is the same white circle, so tell characters apart by height, garment shape and colour, and one accessory, never by facial features. Basis: DeepMind's 'assign a distinct name', traditional comparison sheets, and Google's note about left/right confusion.

Sheet prompt (the owner's one-image requirement): for each script, write one 'Cast & Pose Sheet' prompt that produces a single 16:9 image, structured like Google's notebook (Scene, Setting, rows, Text). Use a flat pure white background. Row 1 is the cast lineup: each character in front view, side by side, feet on one shared ground line, same scale, main character first as the height reference, name label underneath. The next row or two show every pose the script uses, each labelled 'NAME - pose' in quotes. The last row shows only the expression heads the script uses. Every figure is complete and not overlapping, with even spacing and no scenery. Include left and right side views of the main character. Basis: Google's notebook, its side-view note, comparison-sheet practice, and DeepMind's quote rule for text.

Sheet size and budget: put at most 4 named characters (animals included) on a sheet, or 5 if using Pro. As a starting budget to test, not a proven limit, use about 12-14 full-body figures plus about 12 expression heads. That matches the density of the third-party reference. Generate at 2K (2752x1536) or 4K. With the same layout, 2K gives each item about 1.7 times the pixels of the 1644x910 reference: roughly 550 px per full-body figure and 175 px per head. 1K gives about 0.84 times: roughly 275 px and 90 px, where Google says small faces and text blur. Gemini app downloads are 1K without a paid plan. Count figures and labels on every sheet, because the model does not always produce the exact number asked for.

When the script needs more than the budget: keep one image, but first drop turnaround views the script never uses and keep expression heads for the main character only. Split onto a second sheet only as a last resort, and tell the owner when you do.

Build the sheet in stages: (1) a text-only style anchor of the main character on white, approved by the owner; (2) the cast lineup, with the anchor attached as Image 1; (3) the full Cast & Pose Sheet, with the lineup attached. Fix an off-model figure with one targeted edit ('change only the figure labelled ...'), or regenerate that figure alone and paste it in with an editor. The approved result is still one image. Basis: Google's advice to attach earlier outputs, the notebook workflow, and practitioners who assemble views separately.

Sheet checklist before use: check every figure for the white circular head, dot eyes and line mouth; no nose, ears or hair; mitten hands; the same outline weight; costume pieces and colours that match the card; one-sided items on the stated side; heights that match the lineup; label spelling; and the figure count. Reject a flawed sheet rather than use it, because every later image inherits its errors.

Scene prompt template, following Google Cloud's references + relationship + new scenario formula. Start with numbered roles: 'Image 1: the approved Cast & Pose Sheet for this video (character reference only).' Optionally add 'Image 2: pose reference cut from Image 1.' and 'Image 3: previous scene; keep its background and lighting.' Then the relationship: 'Draw NAME, the character labelled "NAME" in Image 1, exactly as drawn there: same head, face, outline weight, clothing, colours and proportions.' Then the new scenario: action, pose, position in frame, camera, props, and explicit removals such as 'NAME is no longer holding the spear'. Then: 'Draw only the characters named here; do not reproduce the sheet's layout, labels or other figures.' Finish with the STYLE BLOCK and '16:9 landscape'. Basis: Google's notebook and DeepMind's naming advice; the 'do not reproduce' line guards against the copy-from-input failure in the model cards.

Attachments: attach the master sheet to every generation that needs consistent characters. Add at most one pose crop and one previous scene. Stay at 4 or fewer character images per request on 2.1 (the Gemini app also caps a prompt at 10 files). The output takes the aspect ratio of the input image, the last one when several are attached, so attach the 16:9 sheet last and also write '16:9 landscape'.

Pose crops: if the scene needs a pose that is on the sheet, cut that one figure from the approved sheet and attach it as the pose reference, as Google advises for complex poses. If the pose is not on the sheet, attach no pose crop, because 2.1 can keep the pose of the input image. Describe the pose in words and add it to the next sheet.

Edit or regenerate: for one local defect (a hand, a prop, an expression), make one targeted edit in the same chat with Google's template: 'change only [X] ... Keep everything else in the image exactly the same, preserving the original style, lighting, and composition.' Stop after 2-3 chained edits; quality degrades with long edit chains. If identity, costume or style is wrong, regenerate from Image 1 in a new chat.

Chat hygiene: use one chat for each batch of about 5-8 images that share a location or chapter, and start each batch in a new chat with the sheet attached again. Start a new chat whenever outputs go back to older images, ignore the reference, or start looking cleaner and more polished. Review each batch side by side against the sheet, not one image at a time. Basis: Google's Developers Blog, plus three practitioner reports.

Wording for minimal features: say what the face is before what it lacks, for example 'the face is only two dots and a short line; the rest of the circle is plain white', then add the short 'Never add' line. Write 'small white oval mitten hands' rather than 'no fingers'; the model turned 'no fingers' into mittens anyway. For expressions, name the exact marks, for example 'two short slanted eyebrow strokes, downturned line mouth'.

Left and right: state the facing direction and every one-sided detail from the character's own side in each prompt, for example 'facing right, pouch on his left hip'. Keep left and right side views on the sheet, and check every output for flips. Prefer symmetric costumes for recurring characters. Basis: Google's model cards list left/right confusion, the notebook needed side views, and the vendor test saw a cap brim flip.

Style across scenes: keep three fixed pieces per video and reuse them word for word: the STYLE BLOCK; a PALETTE line with named colours, hex values as rough hints, and one background description (for example 'flat warm off-white paper, simple flat ground line'); and the cast sheet. Make the first scene of each video carefully and attach it as the previous scene for the next ones, so background, lighting and palette carry over. Hex colours come out only approximately, so correct exact colours afterwards. Pro can also take up to 3 style references if needed.

Animals and recurring props: put recurring animals on the cast sheet as cast members; they count toward the 4-character limit. Describe them with the STYLE BLOCK vocabulary (same outline weight, flat earth-tone fills, dot eyes, simple shapes) and avoid realism words such as 'fur texture' or 'anatomically accurate'. Put recurring props on the sheet, or on a separate prop sheet as Google's notebook suggests, because details that are not shown or described change between runs. I found no direct source for animals, so this needs testing.

Labels and text: keep sheet labels short, in quotes, in one described lettering style ('plain black hand-lettered capitals'), and large enough at 2K; check spelling and redo the lettering in an editor if needed. Scene images should carry no lettering at all, phrased positively ('all signs and surfaces are blank'); captions are added later in Remotion. Basis: blurry small text at 1K, mixed fonts in the xkcd test, and numerals added despite 'no numbers'.

Cut-out prompts: for character-only images meant to be cut out, ask for a 'flat, uniform pure chroma-green (#00FF00) background filling the whole frame; no floor, ground line, cast shadow, gradient or glow; the whole figure visible with a clear margin, not touching the edges'. Our white, black and earth-tone characters contain no green. Switch to magenta #FF00FF when the character or props contain green, such as plants or leaves. Never write 'transparent', because the model paints a fake checkerboard.

Background colour choice: do not use white for cut-outs. The heads and hands are white, so removing white by colour would delete them and leave white pockets between limbs and body; white works only with an AI background remover and checking each image. Avoid grey, which is close to the muted grey-brown clothing (my reasoning, not tested). Keep the reference sheet itself on white, which matches the style and Google's own sheet practice.

Cut-out script: take the background colour from the four corners, because the model returns a near-green, not exact #00FF00. Remove that colour with a tolerance range, clean green spill from edge pixels, and tighten or widen the mask by 1-2 px. Preview each cut-out on dark and light backgrounds and check thin outlines and enclosed gaps. Optional route for softer edges: edit the same image so only the background turns pure black, then compute transparency from the white/black pair. Use it only if the two images line up pixel for pixel.

Watermark: on free or Google AI Pro accounts the Gemini app adds a visible sparkle in the bottom-right corner. Keep characters and key content out of that corner in every prompt. Crop the sparkle off the sheet before re-attaching it, because the model sometimes copies parts of input images into outputs (my precaution, not tested). Plan the Remotion crop accordingly.
Frame resolution: for 2560x1440 frames, generate at 2K 16:9 (2752x1536) and scale down. A 1K image (1376x768) would have to be upscaled, and free Gemini app accounts only get 1K downloads.

Flow workflow: upload the approved sheet once and give it a clear name (for example cast_sheet_ep003). Reference it with Add to Prompt or @name, set 16:9, choose Nano Banana 2.1, and generate 2-4 versions per prompt to pick the one closest to the sheet. Earlier versions stay in the image's history.

Record keeping: save each approved sheet with its exact prompt, tool, model, date and STYLE BLOCK version in the video folder, as Google's notebook does by storing the prompt in PNG metadata. This lets a sheet be regenerated or traced later.
Language: write all image prompts, labels and names in English. English is among Google's best-supported languages, and one language keeps the STYLE BLOCK stable.

Test before locking the templates: for each channel, generate one sheet at 2K, then 10 scenes with the sheet attached. Log every failure type (nose, hair or fingers added; costume change; colour shift; left/right flip; labels leaking into scenes; style polishing). Use the log to tune the 'Never add' line and the figure budget.
